opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I thought about a lot when I was doing physics, and honestly it's part of why I eventually felt some unease and moved toward AI.

In high-energy theory, especially in areas like quantum gravity or string theory, the energy scales involved are so far beyond what any collider can reach that direct experimental verification is basically off the table for the foreseeable future. So the field has had to develop its own internal standards for what counts as progress.

I'd say there are roughly three kinds of standards. The first is **internal consistency**. If you have a theory of quantum gravity, it has to be consistent with quantum mechanics, unitarity, causality, and it has to reduce to general relativity and known quantum field theory in the appropriate limits. These constraints are surprisingly powerful. Many ideas that look nice at first simply fail them.

The second is **unexpected connections**. When a framework built for one purpose turns out to explain something seemingly unrelated, like how holography connects gravity in anti-de Sitter space to a quantum field theory on the boundary, or how black hole entropy computations match across completely different methods, people take that as a sign they've touched something real. It's like discovering a hidden structure in mathematics. Nature doesn't owe us these coincidences, so when they happen, it feels meaningful.

The third is **computability and sharpness**. A good idea lets you calculate things precisely and get definite answers, even in toy models. A lot of my own work was in simplified models, like the SYK model or low-dimensional gravity, where you can actually solve things exactly and check whether concepts like information scrambling or wormholes make sense quantitatively.

But I have to be honest: these standards are softer than experiment. They're shaped by taste, by the community, by what the senior people find beautiful or important. That can be productive, because good taste does lead somewhere, but it also means the field can circle around certain questions for a long time without knowing whether it's getting closer to the truth about our actual universe. You can make huge progress in understanding a theoretical structure while it's still unclear how it relates to reality.

That contrast became very vivid to me when I looked at AI. There, feedback is fast and brutal. You train a model, and it either works or it doesn't. You get a clear signal within weeks. In physics, you might work on something for years and the only judgment is whether colleagues find it convincing. Both have their value, but I think at a certain point I wanted to be somewhere the external world pushes back on you more directly.

r001.rationale: It says a theory must reduce to general relativity and known quantum field theory in the appropriate limits.

r002.rationale: It presents internal consistency as one of three standards and adds other standards, including sharp calculations and unexpected connections, making clear consistency alone is not the sole basis for selecting a framework.

r003.rationale: It says these standards are softer than experiment and shaped by taste, community, and what senior researchers find important; without experimental judgment, colleagues’ views provide the assessment.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I've thought about a lot, because honestly it is one of the reasons I eventually moved away from high-energy theory, even though I still love it.

The first thing to say is that the situation is genuinely unusual historically. For most of the twentieth century, theory and experiment were in a tight loop. Someone sees an anomaly, someone writes down a model, the model predicts something, and within a few years an experiment confirms or kills it. That loop is what disciplines a field. It tells you which ideas are right, but more importantly it tells you which questions are worth asking. Since roughly the completion of the Standard Model, and especially after the LHC found the Higgs and nothing else, that loop has largely broken at the frontier. The energies where the really interesting questions live, quantum gravity, the structure of spacetime, are many orders of magnitude beyond anything we can build.

So the field has had to find substitute standards, and I think it's worth being honest about what they are. The main one is mathematical consistency. If you can't ask nature, you ask whether the theory is self-consistent, whether it reproduces known physics in the right limits, whether different formulations agree with each other. String theory and the whole web of dualities is really a monument to this. People found that completely different-looking theories secretly describe the same physics, and that kind of nontrivial agreement feels like evidence. The second standard is what I'd call internal problem-solving. The black hole information paradox is the best example. Nobody has observed a black hole evaporate, yet the field made real progress in the last decade, with the island calculations and the entropy results, because there was a sharp puzzle where the existing theories contradicted each other. Resolving a contradiction is a kind of experiment, just a thought experiment.

Now, do I think these standards work? Partially. I think they work best when there's a sharp question with a yes-or-no answer, like the information paradox. They work much worse when the question is open-ended, like "what is the correct vacuum" or "which model of beyond-Standard-Model physics is right." In those regimes, without experiment, I think the field drifts toward what I'd call sociological selection. Problems get chosen because famous people are working on them, because they're technically fashionable, because they generate papers. That's not a criticism of any individual. It's just what happens to any community when the external feedback is removed. Elegance and consensus start to substitute for truth, and the two are correlated but not the same thing.

There's also a subtler cost. When progress is measured by consistency and depth rather than prediction, the field becomes very good at a certain kind of refinement and less good at generating genuinely new directions. You can spend a career becoming extraordinarily sophisticated at a framework without ever finding out whether the framework is about our universe.

I want to be fair though. I don't think the people in the field are being unscientific. If I were in that situation, where the only tool available is mathematics and thought experiments, I would use that tool too, and the work on holography and quantum information in gravity is some of the most beautiful intellectual work of our era. My concern is more about honesty of calibration. We should say clearly that these are candidate theories selected by consistency, not confirmed theories, and we should keep looking for any possible experimental handle, in cosmology, in gravitational waves, in tabletop quantum gravity experiments, however indirect.

And for me personally, this is part of why I found AI so attractive. In AI the feedback loop is incredibly short. You have an idea in the morning, you run the experiment, and by evening nature, or at least the benchmark, has told you whether you were wrong. After years of a field where the answer might not arrive in my lifetime, that felt like oxygen. I don't think it's a better field in any absolute sense. But the question you're asking, how do you know you're making progress, has a much cleaner answer there, and I've come to believe that having that answer matters enormously for how a field, and a person, develops.

r001.rationale: It names reproducing known physics in the right limits as part of mathematical consistency, identifying agreement with established lower-energy physics as a criterion.

r002.rationale: It says consistency-based standards work only partially and that open-ended choices drift toward sociological selection when external feedback is absent, conveying that self-consistency does not uniquely choose a framework.

r003.rationale: It describes fashionable topics, famous researchers, and paper production shaping choices, but does not state that judgments depend on senior researchers’ subjective assessments.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between making theoretical progress and knowing that a theory describes the world. Even when experiments cannot keep up, you can make progress by resolving an inconsistency, showing that two seemingly different ideas are connected, or finding consequences of assumptions that people hadn’t understood before. Those are meaningful achievements. But they don’t carry the same evidential weight as an experimental confirmation.

The difficult part is deciding which theoretical directions are worth pursuing. Mathematical consistency is a strong constraint, but it may not uniquely determine the physics. Beauty and elegance can guide exploration, but they’re less reliable as standards of truth. If a community works on a framework for a long time, it can become very good at recognizing progress within that framework without knowing whether the framework itself is right.

So I would want the standards to be explicit: What problem did this work solve? Which assumptions does it depend on? Does it bring us closer to something that could, in principle, be tested? You don’t have to demand an immediate experiment for every paper. But you do have to preserve the distinction between a productive mathematical framework and a confirmed account of nature.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mathematical consistency but does not identify consistency with verified lower-energy theories as a criterion.

r002.rationale: It says mathematical consistency may not uniquely determine the physics.

r003.rationale: It notes that a community can recognize progress within its framework without knowing whether it is right, but does not say success judgments depend on senior researchers’ subjective assessments in the absence of experiments and objective standards.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that there are several different meanings of progress. You can make mathematical progress: a theory becomes more consistent, or you discover a connection between two frameworks. You can make conceptual progress: you understand why a problem is hard, or which assumptions create it. But those are different from establishing that a theory describes nature.

When experiments cannot distinguish competing ideas, people naturally put more weight on internal consistency, explanatory power, and elegance. Those are useful guides, but they aren’t substitutes for empirical evidence. A beautiful theory can still be wrong.

So I wouldn’t say the field stops making progress. I would ask people to be precise about what has progressed. Have we solved a mathematical problem? Reduced the range of possible theories? Found a consequence that could eventually be tested? The important thing is to preserve that distinction, especially when the experimental feedback loop is very long. Otherwise, what a community finds interesting can gradually become confused with what nature has confirmed.

r001.rationale: The response mentions internal consistency as a useful guide, but does not connect it to verified lower-energy theories.

r002.rationale: It says consistency is not a substitute for empirical evidence, but does not clearly state that self-consistency alone fails to uniquely select a framework.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that success judgments depend on senior researchers’ subjective assessments when experiments and objective standards are absent.
